## ISS Data Analytics Project 1
This single-page Python report follows the data preparation, variable definitions, descriptive analysis, correlation analysis, and Mahalanobis-distance workflow in [the updated Python notebook](https://github.com/chipojaya1/ISS-Economic-Distance/blob/main/Economic_distance_analysis.ipynb). The sensitivity analysis is a separate extension. The report adapts an original collaborative empirical project by **Chipo Jaya and Xianghan Zhu**. It provides context for SDG 17 but does **not** directly measure official Target 17.11.
:::

## 1. Research question and data

**How do income, inflation, and international trade contribute to economic distance between the United States and other economies in 2019?**

The data come from the [World Bank World Development Indicators](https://databank.worldbank.org/source/world-development-indicators). We use GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$), GDP-deflator inflation (annual %), imports (% GDP), and exports (% GDP).

```{python}
#| label: data-preparation
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy.spatial.distance import mahalanobis
from IPython.display import display

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
raw = pd.read_excel("data/WDI_Raw_2019.xlsx", sheet_name="Data", na_values=["..", "."])
mapping = {"NY.GDP.PCAP.KD":"gdp_per_capita",
           "NY.GDP.DEFL.KD.ZG":"inflation",
           "NE.IMP.GNFS.ZS":"imports",
           "NE.EXP.GNFS.ZS":"exports"}
features = list(mapping.values())
data = raw.loc[raw["Series Code"].isin(mapping),
               ["Country Name","Country Code","Series Code","2019 [YR2019]"]].copy()
data["value"] = pd.to_numeric(data["2019 [YR2019]"], errors="coerce")
if data.duplicated(["Country Code","Series Code"]).any():
    raise ValueError("Duplicate country-indicator records: inspect source data.")
wide = data.pivot(index=["Country Name","Country Code"],
                  columns="Series Code",values="value").reset_index().rename(columns=mapping)
wide.columns.name = None
wide = wide.rename(columns={"Country Name":"country","Country Code":"iso3c"})
complete = wide.dropna(subset=features).copy()
assert (complete["iso3c"] == "USA").sum() == 1
print(f"Source rows: {len(raw)}; economies: {len(wide)}; complete cases: {len(complete)}")
```

## 2. Sample coverage and missing data

The data include World Bank geographic economies, some of which are not sovereign countries. The analysis follows the notebook's complete-case sample; it does not independently filter the sample to sovereign states. We exclude records missing any of the four indicators for distance calculations.

```{python}
#| label: missingness
coverage = pd.DataFrame({
  "Indicator": features,
  "Available": [wide[col].notna().sum() for col in features],
  "Missing": [wide[col].isna().sum() for col in features]})
display(coverage)
```

## 3. Exploratory data analysis

```{python}
#| label: descriptives
display(complete[features].describe().T[
    ["count","mean","50%","std","min","max"]].rename(columns={"50%":"median"}).round(2))
```

We look at each measure separately to see how economies differ in 2019. Each chart shows the number of economies falling within a particular range. Taller bars mean more economies are in that range.

### GDP per capita — economic output per person

```{python}
#| label: distribution-gdp
#| fig-cap: "GDP per capita across economies in 2019 (constant 2015 US dollars)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
sns.histplot(complete["gdp_per_capita"], bins=28, ax=ax, color="#277c69")
ax.set(xlabel="GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$)", ylabel="Number of economies")
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter, MultipleLocator
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(MultipleLocator(50000))
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda value, _: f"${value/1000:,.0f}k" if value else "$0"))
ax.set_xlim(left=0)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Most economies are clustered toward the lower end of income per person, while a smaller number have much higher GDP per capita. This illustrates how uneven economic output per person was across the economies in the dataset. The horizontal axis shows actual dollar amounts, so the handful of very high values stretches the chart and makes the lower-income economies appear closer together.

### Inflation — how quickly prices were changing

```{python}
#| label: distribution-inflation
#| fig-cap: "GDP-deflator inflation across economies in 2019."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
sns.histplot(complete["inflation"], bins=35, ax=ax, color="#277c69")
ax.set(xlabel="Inflation, GDP deflator (annual %)", ylabel="Number of economies")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

For most economies, inflation was relatively modest in 2019. A few had exceptionally high rates, making the full chart look stretched. This reminds us that the experience of rapid price increases was not shared equally. Here, inflation is measured using the GDP deflator, rather than a household shopping-basket price index.

### Imports — goods and services bought from abroad

```{python}
#| label: distribution-imports
#| fig-cap: "Imports of goods and services as a share of GDP in 2019."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
sns.histplot(complete["imports"], bins=28, ax=ax, color="#277c69")
ax.set(xlabel="Imports (% of GDP)", ylabel="Number of economies")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Some economies relied more heavily on goods and services purchased from other countries than others did. Many were grouped in the middle of the chart, while a smaller number had particularly large import shares. This measure describes the size of imports relative to the economy, not whether imports are good or bad.

### Exports — goods and services sold abroad

```{python}
#| label: distribution-exports
#| fig-cap: "Exports of goods and services as a share of GDP in 2019."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.5))
sns.histplot(complete["exports"], bins=28, ax=ax, color="#277c69")
ax.set(xlabel="Exports (% of GDP)", ylabel="Number of economies")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Economies also differed in how much they sold to the rest of the world compared with the size of their own economies. Most had more moderate export shares, whereas a few stood out with especially high shares. High export shares can be common in economies that are deeply connected to international trade.

### How the four measures relate to one another

The charts above show each measure on its own. The next chart looks at whether economies with higher values on one measure also tend to have higher values on another.

```{python}
#| label: correlations
#| fig-cap: "Pearson correlation matrix of the four economic indicators."
correlations = complete[features].corr()
fig,ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5.5))
sns.heatmap(correlations,annot=True,fmt=".2f",center=0,cmap="BrBG",
            vmin=-1,vmax=1,ax=ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Imports and exports as percentages of GDP are strongly associated in the study sample. Correlation is descriptive and does not establish causality.

## 4. Measuring economic distance

### Why use Mahalanobis distance?

A simple comparison might focus on how far two economies differ in each indicator. However, GDP per capita is measured in dollars while the other indicators are percentages. Imports and exports also tend to move together. **Mahalanobis distance** takes these differences in scale and the relationships between indicators into account, allowing us to summarize the four measures in one comparison.

$$D(x,US)=\sqrt{(x-x_{US})^T S^{-1}(x-x_{US})}$$

Here $S$ is the covariance matrix calculated from the same complete-case sample. The United States is the reference economy, so its distance from itself is zero. **Smaller distances indicate greater similarity to the United States across these four selected indicators; they do not imply better economic performance.**

### Which economies are most similar to or different from the United States?

```{python}
#| label: distances
X = complete[features].to_numpy(dtype=float)
cov = np.cov(X, rowvar=False)
inverse = np.linalg.inv(cov)
us = complete.loc[complete.iso3c.eq("USA"), features].iloc[0].to_numpy(dtype=float)
complete["distance_us"] = [mahalanobis(x, us, inverse) for x in X]
ranked = complete.loc[complete.iso3c.ne("USA")].sort_values("distance_us")
closest = ranked[["country", "distance_us"]].head(5)
furthest = ranked[["country", "distance_us"]].tail(5).sort_values("distance_us", ascending=False)
print("Five economies closest to the United States")
display(closest.round(3).reset_index(drop=True))
print("Five economies furthest from the United States")
display(furthest.round(3).reset_index(drop=True))
```

In the baseline results, **Australia, Norway, and the United Kingdom** are the three closest economies to the United States. Their combined income, inflation, and trade profiles are relatively similar to the US profile according to this measure. Iceland and Canada follow.

At the other end, **Venezuela, Djibouti, and Hong Kong SAR, China** have the greatest distances. The fact that Luxembourg also appears among the most distant illustrates an important point: the distance measure does not simply separate rich from poor economies. Very high shares of international trade can contribute to a distinctive economic profile.

### Visual comparison of the extremes

```{python}
#| label: distance-chart
#| fig-cap: "Five closest and five most distant economies relative to the United States, 2019."
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8.5))
for ax, subset, heading, color in [
    (axes[0], closest.iloc[::-1], "Closest to the United States", "#277c69"),
    (axes[1], furthest.iloc[::-1], "Most distant from the United States", "#b46c51")
]:
    ax.barh(subset["country"], subset["distance_us"], color=color)
    ax.set_title(heading, loc="left", fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlabel("Mahalanobis distance (no units)")
    ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.2)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_xlim(0, subset["distance_us"].max()*1.2)
    for i, value in enumerate(subset["distance_us"]):
        ax.text(value + subset["distance_us"].max()*.025, i, f"{value:.2f}",
                va="center", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=2)
plt.show()
```

These distances are relative comparisons, **not percentages or probabilities**. A score of 6, for example, does not mean an economy is six times poorer, richer, or less developed than the United States.

### What should we be careful about?

The results depend on the four indicators selected, the economies with complete data, and the way extreme values influence the covariance calculation. Venezuela's unusually high 2019 inflation is especially important to consider. We cannot tell from the overall distance score alone exactly how much of a country's ranking is explained by each indicator.

The next section checks how rankings change when extreme observations are treated differently. The analysis remains descriptive: it measures similarity in selected economic characteristics, not the causes of those differences.

## 5. Sensitivity to outliers

To assess how extreme values influence results, the four indicators are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles and the covariance matrix is recalculated. This is an alternative specification, not a replacement for the baseline.

```{python}
#| label: sensitivity
adjusted=complete[features].copy()
for col in features:
    low,high=adjusted[col].quantile([.01,.99])
    adjusted[col]=adjusted[col].clip(lower=low,upper=high)
Xa=adjusted.to_numpy(dtype=float)
inva=np.linalg.inv(np.cov(Xa,rowvar=False))
usa=adjusted.loc[complete.iso3c.eq("USA")].iloc[0].to_numpy(dtype=float)
complete["adjusted_distance_us"]=[mahalanobis(x,usa,inva) for x in Xa]
comparison=complete.loc[complete.iso3c.ne("USA"),
                        ["country","distance_us","adjusted_distance_us"]].copy()
comparison["original_rank"]=comparison.distance_us.rank(method="min")
comparison["adjusted_rank"]=comparison.adjusted_distance_us.rank(method="min")
comparison["rank_change"]=comparison.adjusted_rank-comparison.original_rank
display(comparison.loc[comparison.rank_change.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index].head(10).round(2))
```

## 6. Conclusions and limitations

Differences across economies depend on indicator selection, missing-data exclusions, and statistical treatment of unusually large observations. This is a single-year descriptive analysis, not causal evidence. The original sample includes economies rather than only sovereign states. Results should not be used on their own to infer regulatory similarity or identify the best investment destination.

**Replication note:** The source notebook identifies GDP per capita as `gdp_per_capita` and the two trade indicators as `imports` and `exports`; these names are now used consistently in this report. The sensitivity check below is an additional analysis, not a result established by the source notebook.

**SDG relevance:** Exports and imports support a broader discussion of international trade and SDG 17. They are not a direct estimate of the official Target 17.11 indicator, developing countries' share of global exports.
